blocks.html: Chapter 16 asked whether one instrument measures what it claims to. This chapter asks the same question of a whole study: even with a perfect instrument and a correct calculation, can the design or conduct of the study give a wrong answer? It sets out the three alternative explanations for an observed association (§17.1), the systematic errors of selection and measurement with a catalogue of the named biases and Bradford Hill’s viewpoints (§17.2), confounding and what design can do about it, with quantitative bias analysis and the E-value (§17.3). It closes with the two skills that turn a valid study into a usable paper: reporting it to the standard of the reporting guidelines (§17.4), and knowing enough qualitative and mixed methods to work alongside them (§17.5).
